carried at run time is that name, a string in the representation but **not** in the type.

`T` names one **class**. An interface, an enum, a scalar, a `class<...>` — anything that is not a
class — is `E0799` where it is written, and so is a class declaring no public property at all, since
no value of that type could exist. The interface row is the conservative one: a key's set has to be a
roster the receiver certainly has storage for, and an interface names a contract its implementors
satisfy with properties it does not itself declare. The set is the same roster reflection walks; the
visibility question has one shared implementation and this is not a second one.

**`as` is its source, and a literal at a key parameter is the other.** A string literal is a `string`
and stays one everywhere but that one position, so no program acquires a key by accident. Three rows sit in the one conversion grid ([`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion)): a `string` must name
a public declared property of `T`, or it throws; a `property<U>` narrows at run time; and
`property<T> → string` is total. A name that names nothing and a name that names a `private` property
are the same failure and throw the same way — visibility is decided at the conversion, once. A
written-out operand is decided **where it is written**: `"email" as property<User>` is a compile-time
yes, or the same unknown-member diagnostic an ordinary `$user->emial` gets. `as ?property<T>` yields
`null` where the checked form throws.

A qualifier is stripped for a reason narrower than the general row's: the conversion's whole output
range is the set of properties `User` declares `public` in this program's own source. A tainted string
cannot widen that set, name a field the author did not write down, or reach a `private` one.

A parameter typed **`property<T>|string`** takes a key and any string. A string literal written there
stays a `string`, and the body converts the value with `as ?property<T>` to find out whether it names one
of `T`'s properties. The editor offers `T`'s names inside such a literal
([`ide/completion-offers-only-what-the-compiler-derived`](ide.md#ide-completion-offers-only-what-the-compiler-derived)), so a call site that may pass any string is
still shown the names.

A parameter typed **`property<T>` alone**, or `?property<T>`, takes a key, and a **string literal**
written there is converted while compiling. A right one is accepted with no `as`, and a wrong one is
the unknown-member diagnostic at the literal: the check `"email" as property<User>` makes where it is
written, and not a second one. A string built at run time still needs `as`, so no program acquires a
key from a value the compiler has not seen. In a variable, a return and an array a literal stays a
`string`. This is the position where a name is wanted and the literal is the whole of what the call
site says: making the caller write `as property<User>` there repeats the class the signature already
names, and the editor offers the names there too. [`types/property-path`](types.md#types-property-path) and
[`types/string-holes`](types.md#types-string-holes) apply the same position to `propertyPath<T>` and `string<K>`.

It is its own **equality domain**: two keys are equal when they name the same property, nothing else is
ever equal to one, and ordering one is refused ([`types/ordering`](types.md#types-ordering)). `property` is a keyword only
in type position — `$property`, a method named `property` and a class named `Property` are untouched.

The type exists because the refusal of `$obj->$name` alone leaves three bad options for a request that
names a field — a sort column, a patch document's key, a form input. A hand-written `match` the
compiler cannot check covers the class; an `array<string, T>` beside the object gives up the declared
types; and reflection returns `mixed` and moves every check to run time. Each re-derives a fact the
compiler already has: the class's property roster is finite, declared and known
([`classes/no-dynamic-properties`](classes.md#classes-no-dynamic-properties)). The bound a key sets is narrower than the `match`, because the
compiler cannot tell whether one arm of the `match` was mistyped. A key is not a replacement for
`array<string, mixed>`: a program that wants arbitrary keys still wants an array, and a key is for
fields that are the class's own when the choice among them is made late.

The run-time conversion is one field lookup and one visibility test, the pair reflection already
performs, once where the string arrives. A written-out operand skips it. The value is a name and not a
slot index: an index would bind the key to one class's field layout, while a key is applied to
receivers of every subclass ([`types/property-key-variance`](types.md#types-property-key-variance)), and the lookup an index would save
is one the erased access performs anyway.

- **Memory:** a key is one string value, the property's name. Nothing is added to the class
  descriptor, and nothing is spent per request or per instance.

**Declined:**
- **Keep the refusal and offer nothing.** It pushes the ordinary program onto a `match` the compiler
  cannot check or an array that erases the declared types, both with less checking than the syntax it
  replaces.
- **Hooked and `readonly` properties left out of the set.** "The public properties" would become two
  rosters, this one and reflection's. Adding a hook to a property later would also turn a working `as`
  into a run-time throw in a file that did not change. The `readonly` half is refused at the write
  instead ([`types/property-key-access`](types.md#types-property-key-access)).
- **A `Core` function that takes a property name and a class as two strings.** It checks only at run
  time and gives back a value the checker cannot type, so the read is `mixed` and the write is
  unchecked. A type is the only shape that reaches the access site.
- **A bare `string` accepted at `$obj->$name` when the class is written out.** The check moves from the
  source to every use, so an unchecked string flows through the program.
- **Converting a literal wherever a key is expected, in a variable or a return too.** A literal in a
  variable has no single expected type until it is used, so the rule would depend on inference order.
  The argument position has its type written in the signature.
- **Checking a literal at a `property<T>|string` parameter as well.** That parameter says any string is
  fine, and a warning there would be noise at every call that passes free text.
- **A key that may name a `private` property, with visibility checked at the access.** The conversion
  would succeed on a name the caller may not use, and the throw would land at a site that looks
  correct. Visibility belongs to the set, so it is checked where the set is entered.

<sub>See also [`types/property-key-variance`](types.md#types-property-key-variance), [`types/property-key-access`](types.md#types-property-key-access), [`types/class-reference`](types.md#types-class-reference), [`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion).</sub>

<a id="types-property-key-variance"></a>

## `property<T>` widens as `T` narrows, because the argument bounds the receiver

`rule:types/property-key-variance`

A subclass *adds* properties, so `property<Animal>`'s names are all valid on a `Dog` while
`property<Dog>`'s are not all valid on an `Animal`. **`property<Animal>` therefore widens to
`property<Dog>`, and never back**: the argument is contravariant.

That is exactly opposite to `class<T>` ([`types/class-reference-variance`](types.md#types-class-reference-variance)), and for the reason
that inverts it — a class reference is *produced* against its bound, while a key is *consumed* by a
receiver. Narrowing is written like every other narrowing, `as property<Animal>`, and is the run-time
check the conversion's second row already describes.

The rule at the site follows and adds nothing: `$obj->$key` requires `$obj`'s type to be a `T`, where
`T` is the key's argument. A key made against `Animal` reads a `Dog`; a key made against `Dog` does not
read an `Animal`.

**Declined:**
- **`property<T>` covariant, like `class<T>`.** It reads as the obvious rule and is unsound: a
  `property<Dog>` passed where `property<Animal>` is wanted lets `$breed` reach an `Animal` receiver,
  which has no such storage.

<sub>See also [`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key), [`types/class-reference-variance`](types.md#types-class-reference-variance), [`types/property-key-access`](types.md#types-property-key-access).</sub>

<a id="types-property-key-access"></a>

## `$obj->$key` accepts a `property<T>` and nothing else; a read is the union and a write is checked

`rule:types/property-key-access`

`$obj->$key` and `$obj->{$expr}` are admitted, and **only** when the operand's type is a `property<T>`
whose argument the receiver satisfies ([`types/property-key-variance`](types.md#types-property-key-variance)). Every other operand keeps
`E0235`, with its help naming `as property<T>`, and the refusal lives in the checker rather than the
parser, because the operand's *type* is the question and the parser cannot see one. The spelling is no
longer what is rejected; the missing check is.

Three neighbours stay exactly as they are: `$obj->$m(...)` is `E0235` forever, because computed
*dispatch* is rejected as a concept and a key is not a method name; `$obj->$key` on a `mixed` or
shape-typed receiver is `E0235`, because there is no `T` to check the key's bound against; and
`unset($obj->$key)` is `E0234`, as `unset` of any property already is.

A **read** through a key is typed as the **union of the set's declared types** — `int|string|?Address`
for a `User` declaring those three — which widens into `mixed` or any covering union without an `as`
and narrows the way every union narrows ([`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed)).

A **write** is the checked erased store ([`types/erased-member-access`](types.md#types-erased-member-access)): it writes an existing
property, never creates one, and the incoming value is checked at run time against what the class
declares that property to hold. Statically the value must satisfy at least one member of the union — a
value no property of `T` could accept is refused where it is written. Both directions lower to the
erased access the runtime already performs, so per-property hooks and a declared property observer
behave exactly as they do there.

**A value that carries `tainted` or `secret` must fit every property the key can name**, and is
`E0401` at the first one it does not fit. Both qualifiers are erased at run time, so the run-time check
sees a `tainted string` and a `string` as the same value: against the union `string|tainted string`
alone, a request's text would land in the plain `string` property and leave it as trusted text. The
same holds for `.=` and `??.=`, whose result is the property's own text with the value appended, and
for `??=`. A value with no qualifier keeps the union check, because the run-time check already refuses
a representation the named property does not hold — so `$stock->$key = 12` still writes the `int`
member of a `string|int` set. An element write through a key needs no more than the union, because
only an `array<T>` can be subscripted and a union of two types is not one. An `inout` argument through
a key is refused (`E0439`): the callee could store a value only some of the properties accept.

**A write is refused, at the write, where `T`'s public set holds a `readonly` property**, naming it
(`E0782`) — the code an ordinary post-construction write already gets. Reading `$id` through a key is
fine, and a class whose fields are all assignable is unaffected. It is deliberately compile-time:
where a request-controlled name selects a field to write, refusing at build time is the direction
security points in.

Applying a key costs exactly what the erased access costs, because it is that access: one call per
direction, with no new descriptor field and no new calling convention. A written-out `$user->email`
pays nothing.

**Declined:**
- **Every write checked against every property, whatever its value.** It refuses a key over a class
  whose properties have different types, which is the case a key exists for. Only a qualifier is
  invisible to the run-time check, so only a qualified value needs the stricter one.
- **A hook entry and a `readonly` flag per field on the class descriptor.** The hook entry buys
  nothing, because the erased access already runs hooks. The flag buys a run-time throw where the
  write above is already refused at compile time.
- **A chain of name tests over the key's set, one ordinary read per public property.** It spends a
  comparison and a basic block per property at every access to reach the slot the erased access finds
  in one call. Each arm's read would also be tagged into the union before the join, so it gives no
  statically typed read.

<sub>See also [`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key), [`types/erased-member-access`](types.md#types-erased-member-access), [`types/property-key-variance`](types.md#types-property-key-variance).</sub>

<a id="types-property-path"></a>

## `propertyPath<T>` is a type whose values are dotted chains of public property names starting at `T`, checked one segment at a time

`rule:types/property-path`

`propertyPath<T>` is a type atom beside `property<T>`, written in every position a type is written,
whose **values** are dotted chains of public declared property names starting at `T`: `customer`,
`customer.address.city`, `lines.product.name`. What is carried at run time is the dotted text, a string
in the representation but **not** in the type.

Every segment but the last names a property whose declared type is a class `C`, a `?C`, or an array of
`C` (`array<C>`), and the next segment is looked up on `C`. The last segment is any public
property. A segment that names nothing, names a `private` or `protected` property, or steps through a
property whose type is not one of those three forms is the same failure, and fails the same way at
every segment. `T` follows [`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key) exactly: one class, `E0799` for anything else or
for a class with no public property; visibility decided at the conversion, once; the argument
contravariant ([`types/property-key-variance`](types.md#types-property-key-variance)); and its own equality domain, two paths equal when
their text is equal, with ordering refused. `propertyPath` is a keyword only in type position, as
`property` is.

**`as` is its source, and a literal at a key parameter is the other** ([`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key)): a string literal at a parameter typed `propertyPath<T>` alone is
converted while compiling.
A `string` converts with `as propertyPath<T>`, which throws at the first bad segment and names it, and
`as ?propertyPath<T>` yields `null` there. A written-out operand is decided where it is written: a
wrong segment is the unknown-member diagnostic an ordinary `$order->custmer` gets, placed on that
segment. `propertyPath<T> → string` is total and gives the dotted text. The conversion strips `tainted` for
the reason [`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key) strips it: its whole output range is chains of names the program
declares `public`.

The run-time conversion costs one field lookup and one visibility test per segment, the pair the key
conversion performs once, and has **no length limit**: a path that names the same relation many times
over is checked one segment at a time, so its cost is linear in what the caller sent and nothing is
held per segment beyond the walk. A path that loops through a class back to itself is legal and costs
the same, because each step reads one class's roster.

The type exists because a field named across a relation — a sort column `customer.name`, a filter
`lines.product.sku`, a form field for a nested object — is otherwise a string the compiler cannot
check, or a chain of `property<T>` keys a library has to join by hand. The roster each step reads is
the one `property<T>` already records per class ([`classes/no-dynamic-properties`](classes.md#classes-no-dynamic-properties)), so a path adds
no second walk.

- **Memory:** a path is one string value, its dotted text. The checker keeps one roster per class a
  path reaches, as `property<T>` does, for the length of the analysis. Nothing is spent per request
  beyond the string, and the run-time conversion allocates nothing past it.

**Declined:**
- **Reading or writing through a path, `$obj->{$path}`, for now.** A path through an array would read
  an array of values, and what that read returns, and what a write through it means, is a decision of
  its own. A library walks the path with `Core\Reflect::steps`
  ([`core-classes/str-parts-and-reflect-steps`](core-classes.md#core-classes-str-parts-and-reflect-steps)) until that is decided.
- **A path as an array of keys, `array<property<T>>`.** Each key would be typed against a different
  class, which no single element type expresses, and a request carries a sort field as one string.
- **A depth limit.** The cost is already linear in the text the caller sent, and the request's own
  limits bound that text. A limit would be a second number to configure with nothing it protects.

<sub>See also [`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key), [`types/property-key-variance`](types.md#types-property-key-variance), [`types/string-holes`](types.md#types-string-holes), [`core-classes/str-parts-and-reflect-steps`](core-classes.md#core-classes-str-parts-and-reflect-steps).</sub>

<a id="types-string-holes"></a>

## `string<K>` is a string whose `{…}` holes are each a `K`, checked where it is written, and its text keeps its taint

`rule:types/string-holes`

`string<K>` is a string with holes: text in which every `{…}` is one value of `K`, checked where the
string is written. `K` is a `property<T>`, a `propertyPath<T>` ([`types/property-path`](types.md#types-property-path)), or a set
of allowed string values ([`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types)). `string<K>` is not a collection, as
`array<K>` is: it is one string, and `K` says what its holes may contain. `string` takes `<` as a type
word only when `<` follows it, the way `property` does, so a plain `string` is untouched.

A hole is `{`, one value of `K`, and `}`, with no spaces inside. `{{` is a literal `{` and `}}` a literal
`}`. An empty hole, an unclosed `{` and a lone `}` are errors, at the brace. Holes work in both quote
styles, because a brace with no `$` after it is already plain text in a string
(`tests/conformance/lang/a-string-literal-escapes-and-interpolates-exactly-what-each-quote-allows.nvst:61`).
A literal at a parameter typed `string<K>` alone is checked where it is written, as a literal at a
`property<T>` parameter is ([`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key)): a wrong hole is the
unknown-member diagnostic for its segment, placed on that segment. A double-quoted string that
interpolates `{$…}` is not a literal, so it needs `as string<K>`, which checks every hole at run time
and throws at the first bad one. `as ?string<K>` yields `null` there. `string<K> → string` is total and
gives the text as written, braces and escapes included.

**Taint stays on the text.** `as string<K>` does not strip `tainted`, unlike `as property<T>` and `as
propertyPath<T>`: the text between the holes is still the caller's text. A `tainted string` converts
to a `tainted string<K>`, and its text pieces are `tainted string` when `Core\Str::parts` splits them
([`core-classes/str-parts-and-reflect-steps`](core-classes.md#core-classes-str-parts-and-reflect-steps)). Only the holes are stripped, because each is a
declared name. A condition built from a request therefore never reaches `Core\Db`'s query text, which
refuses `tainted` ([`core-classes/db-one-api`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-one-api)). This is the security half of the type.

It is its own equality domain: two values are equal when their text is equal, and ordering one is
refused ([`types/ordering`](types.md#types-ordering)).

The type exists because a library that takes a condition, a sort order or a column list as text — a
query builder, a filter, a report — names fields inside that text, and today the compiler sees only a
string. The holes are the part the compiler can check, and Novis parses nothing else: the text between
them is the library's own language.

- **Memory:** a value is one string, its text as written. Checking a literal costs nothing at run time.
  A run-time conversion walks the text once and allocates nothing past the result.

**Declined:**
- **A new word — `format`, `template`, `placeholder`, `path`, `text`.** `Core\Str::format` is the
  `printf` member, `template` reads as an HTML template, a SQL query's `:0` and `?` are placeholders
  ([`core-classes/db-parameters`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-parameters)), and `path` and `text` already mean something. `string<K>` adds no
  word and says what the value is.
- **Stripping `tainted` with the holes.** The text between the holes is the caller's, so a request
  could write SQL into a condition and have it reach query text as trusted.
- **Spaces inside a hole, `{ name }`.** It is a second spelling of the same hole and makes `{ ` in plain
  text ambiguous.

<sub>See also [`types/property-path`](types.md#types-property-path), [`types/property-key`](types.md#types-property-key), [`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types), [`core-classes/str-parts-and-reflect-steps`](core-classes.md#core-classes-str-parts-and-reflect-steps), [`core-classes/db-one-api`](core-classes.md#core-classes-db-one-api).</sub>

<a id="types-unions-and-mixed"></a>

## A union permits only what every member permits, and `mixed` is the one position checked nowhere

`rule:types/unions-and-mixed`

A union permits only the operations valid for *every* member. Reaching a member's own operations means
narrowing ([`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing)), and the spelling that narrows is the `is` operator
([`types/type-test`](types.md#types-type-test)) — never an `is_int()`-style free function, because there are no free
functions, which is also why `Core\Validate` carries no numeric predicates. *Getting* a scalar out of
a union or out of `mixed` is a different question from testing for one: that is `as T`, which throws,
or `as ?T`, which yields `null`. `as` converts and so accepts what can be converted — `"7" as ?int` is
`7` — while `is` reads the representation and so answers `false` for the same value.

A member is one of those operations. A property or a method every class of a union of classes declares
with the same type, and makes visible at the access, is read or called through the union with no
narrowing: [`types/a-member-every-class-of-a-union-declares`](types.md#types-a-member-every-class-of-a-union-declares) is the test, the write and the
lowering. A union whose classes do not all share the member is narrowed first, as any other operation
one member alone allows.

`mixed` is **not checked at all** — that is its entire job. It holds anything, every operation on it
is allowed, and every operation on it is resolved dynamically at runtime through the generic helper
path. That is dynamic typing at dynamic typing's cost, which is the right pressure: the fast path is
the typed one. `Core\Reflect::typeOf` is the one type-introspection member, and it is meaningful only
on a `mixed`, because the checker already knows every other case.

`mixed` is where untyped input lands, deliberately. `Core\Request::json()`, `Core\Script::args()` and
`Core\Json::decode`'s result are `mixed`, because a document genuinely is untyped and pretending
otherwise would be a lie in the type. A request's query and form fields are not: they are text, and
their accessors answer `?tainted string` and `array<tainted string>` ([`security/tainted-sources`](security.md#security-tainted-sources)).
What makes `mixed` safe is that text out of it is `tainted` ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)), while
a number, a `bool` or an enum is proven by its own conversion:

```nvs
mixed $doc = Core\Request::json();
uint $id = $doc['id'] as uint;                    // throws on "abc", on "-1", on "" — never quietly 0
tainted string $q = $doc['q'] as string;
```

`mixed` never absorbs implicitly in the other direction: `int $n = $m;` where `$m` is `mixed` is a
diagnostic, not a runtime check.

`mixed` is a hole by design, and a program written entirely in it runs at dynamic typing's speed with
dynamic typing's failure modes. The compiler does not keep `mixed` at the boundaries; review does, and
every step out of it is an `as` a reviewer can see.

**Declined:**
- **`mixed` checked at its boundaries.** It would leave no way to say "this is untyped input"
  honestly, which is the one thing `mixed` is for.

<sub>See also [`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing), [`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion), [`types/grammar`](types.md#types-grammar), [`types/mixed-subscript`](types.md#types-mixed-subscript), [`types/type-test`](types.md#types-type-test).</sub>

<a id="types-a-member-every-class-of-a-union-declares"></a>

## A union of classes reads and calls a member every class declares with the same type

`rule:types/a-member-every-class-of-a-union-declares`

A property read and a method call through a union of classes compile when every class of the union
declares or inherits that member, the member is visible at the access site in every class, and every
class gives it the same type. `Box|Circle $s; echo $s->name;` compiles when both classes declare
`string $name`. This is [`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed)'s own sentence applied to a member: the
operation is valid for every member of the union, so the union permits it.

- **The same type** is identical, nullability and the `tainted` and `secret` qualifiers included. A
  method's **same signature** is the same parameters with their types, `inout`, defaults and
  variadic, the same return type and the same `static`. The result therefore has one type, and
  nothing after the access depends on which class was behind it.
- **A common parent is not needed and not used.** Two classes that inherit the member from one parent
  share it by the test above; two unrelated classes that each declare it share it the same way.
- **Every member of the union is a class.** An interface in the union keeps `E0477` for a call and
  `E0495` for a property, because an interface has no fixed offset, and the fixed-offset read is what
  the lowering below is. A nullable union follows the nullable rules a single class follows: `?->`
  reads it, and `->` is `E_NULLABLE_RECEIVER`.
- **A write** compiles only when the property is writable at the site in every class: the same type,
  not `readonly` in any class, and the same `set` visibility. A write checks the incoming value
  against one declared type, so a union whose classes agree on that type writes exactly what a write
  through each class would. A union where one class makes the property `readonly` or narrows its
  `set` visibility could not be written through one check, and stays an error. So does a class whose
  property has a `get` hook and no `set` hook. A union where one class hooks the property is no
  `inout` argument and no root of an element write, with the one-class codes `E0439` and `E0478`.
- **`isinit($u->p)`** needs one known class and stays `E0854` through a union.
- **A union of classes that do not share the member** is one new code, `E0881`, whose message names
  the class that lacks the member, the class where it is not visible, or the two types that differ.
  `E0495` and `E0477` stay for a receiver that can hold no object at all, and for a union with a
  non-class member ([`types/a-declared-type-answers-before-the-program-runs`](types.md#types-a-declared-type-answers-before-the-program-runs)).

**The lowering is a class test per class, then the access that class alone makes.** The checker records
each class of the union with its member, and the lowering tests the receiver with `ClassTest` for each
class but the last. Each branch lowers as the same access through that one class does: a fixed-offset
field load for a plain property, the hook for a hooked one, the class's own call for a method. The last
class is the fall-through, because the checker proved the receiver is one of the union's classes.
The field load does not check its receiver's class, so `bun nv soundness` reads a subclass's
redeclared property through a union both from a tested arm and from the fall-through.

- **Latency:** a union of `n` classes pays `n - 1` class tests and the access, with no name lookup
  and no error edge. An access through one class does not change.
- **Memory:** one list of classes per access site in the checker's table, per compiled program and
  never per request.

**Declined:**
- **The name-keyed slot fetch [`types/erased-member-access`](types.md#types-erased-member-access) uses.** It looks the name up on every
  read and adds an error edge for a case the checker already ruled out.
- **Reading through the nearest common parent.** It would accept only unions with such a parent, and a
  member two unrelated classes each declare is the case the `is` ladder this replaces is written for.
- **Interface arms.** A later change can add them through the dispatch a call on an interface already
  uses; refusing them now is the reversible choice.

<sub>See also [`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed), [`types/a-declared-type-answers-before-the-program-runs`](types.md#types-a-declared-type-answers-before-the-program-runs), [`types/erased-member-access`](types.md#types-erased-member-access), [`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing).</sub>

<a id="types-one-mistake-reports-once"></a>

## One mistake in a program reports one error, and a value written as `mixed` keeps every error it has

`rule:types/one-mistake-reports-once`

One mistake in a program reports one error: a name that does not resolve gives its root diagnostic once,
and no later use of it reports again. The checker types every place that has already reported as the
error type. It prints as `mixed` wherever a type is shown, and it is assignable to and from every type.
A member read, a method call, a subscript and an operator on it report nothing and give the error type
again. A union or an intersection with it as a member is the error type.

A value the program *wrote* as `mixed` is not the error type and keeps every error it has
([`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed)): a `mixed` parameter used where a `string` is declared is still `E0401`.
Only the place that reported is quiet.

The skip lives in the report helpers, not at their callers. Every `E0401` goes through one function, and
it returns without reporting when either side is the error type, so a report site added later is quiet
for free and a contributor has nothing to remember. The error-count guards that stop a second report
inside one expression stay.

A check that a declaration fails whatever its types are still reports beside the root error: a
`#[BeforeClass]` method that declares a parameter, a command that is not `static`, a fixture that is not
`public`. Declaring the missing name does not fix it, so it is a second mistake, and a report site is
quiet only where its message would name the error type.

An unresolved `use` reports `E0306` at its own line, and the short name it would have brought in types as
the error type wherever it is written, with no `E0303` there.

The error type never reaches lowering: a program with an error diagnostic does not compile, so `nvs-ir`
meeting it is a compiler bug, and a debug assertion there names this rule.

Why: an editor or a hook that shows the first few errors shows the real ones, and a reader fixes one
line, not every line that repeats it. It costs one type compare per report site, and one interned type
per checker run.

**Declined:**
- **Suppressing by error count alone.** It cannot see past one expression, and it would hide a second,
  independent mistake.
- **Hiding `E0306`.** The `use` line is where the fix is written, so its error is the one to keep.
- **Stopping after the first error.** Two independent mistakes in one program give two errors.

<sub>See also [`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed).</sub>

<a id="types-type-test"></a>

## `$x is T` tests whether a value holds a `T`, answers `bool`, and never refuses because the answer is knowable

`rule:types/type-test`

`$x is T` asks whether a value currently holds a `T` and answers `bool`, for any type a value can
inhabit. It is **strict** — nothing is coerced on the way to the answer — and it is **total**: it
always compiles, and a result the checker can settle by itself folds to a constant rather than
becoming a diagnostic. It is Novis's only type test: there is no second operator for the class case
([`types/one-type-test`](types.md#types-one-type-test)).

The right-hand side is a **type**, parsed by the same production `as` uses
([`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion)), not an expression — with the single exception of § *The value arm* below,
which a `$` opens and nothing else does. `is` is the question `as` was standing in for and never
answered: `"7" as ?int` is `7`, because `string → int` is a conversion row, while `"7" is int` is
`false`, because a `string` is not an `int`. One asks what a value can *become*, the other what it
*is*.

```nvs
mixed $m = Core\Request::json();
if ($m is int) {
    // $m is an int here — no `as`, no throw path
}
```

## What may appear on the right

| form | example |
|---|---|
| a scalar type | `$x is int`, `is uint`, `is float`, `is decimal`, `is string`, `is bytes`, `is bool`, `is null` |
| `object`, a class, an interface | `$x is object`, `$x is Request` |
| an array | `$x is array`, `$x is array<int>` |
| a shape | `$x is {x: int, y: int}` |
| `iterable`, `callable`, a callable signature | `$x is iterable`, `$x is callable` |
| a single-value type | `$x is 5`, `$x is 'yay'`, `$x is true` |
| a class constant or an enum case | `$x is Mode::Read`, `$x is Limits::MAX` |
| an enum | `$x is Rank` |
| `mixed` | `$x is mixed` — always `true`, the wildcard |
| a union or an intersection of any of those | `$x is int\|float`, `$x is Stringable&Comparable` |
| a class reference held in a binding | `$x is $cls` — § *The value arm* |

`array<T>` with a named element type, and a shape, each cost an O(n) walk — the same walk
`as array<T>` already performs, in a spelling that answers instead of throwing. An enum is its cases:
`$x is Rank` answers exactly what asking every `$x is Rank::Case` in turn answers, at one payload
compare per case after one tag comparison, and [`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation) owns what that can tell
apart — a case that reached `mixed` carries an enum tag, so it is told apart from an integer, but not
from another enum's case of the same value and backing. Every other row is one tag comparison, or the descriptor walk
the class-test instruction performs.

There is no `float` single-value type to test against ([`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types)), so `$x is 3.14` is
refused by that rule and not by this one.

## The value arm

A `$` after `is` opens the one arm that is a value rather than a type: `$x is $cls` is the **dynamic
class test**, where `$cls` is a `class<T>` ([`types/class-reference`](types.md#types-class-reference)). It tests the class the
subject holds against the descriptor the reference carries — the same descriptor walk a written class
name lowers to — and narrows the subject to `T` on the true edge. `$x is $this->cls` is the same arm;
every other token after `is` starts a type, which keeps a DNF type's opening `(` a type.

A value on the right that is **not** a `class<T>` is `E0496`, the one report `new $v(...)` and
`$v::f(...)` already share, with its help naming `as class<T>`
([`types/class-reference-sites`](types.md#types-class-reference-sites)). A program that wants a computed class reference binds it to a
local and converts it there; a call or a constant after `is` is read as a type and resolves or fails
as one.

## The refusals

| refused | code | why |
|---|---|---|
| `$x is tainted string`, `is secret bytes` | `E0813` | [`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier) erases both qualifiers before codegen. There is no runtime bit, so the question has no answer — not merely a knowable one. Over a `mixed` or `object` subject `tainted` is admitted and tested as plain text, because there it is the answer [`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation) gives anyway |
| `$x is void`, `$x is never` | `E0811` | no value inhabits either |
| `$c is class<Dog>`, alone or in a union | `E0867` | a class reference carries the class it names and no tag for the `T` it was declared with, so there is no run-time row. `$c as ?class<Dog>` walks the named class and gives `null` when it is not a `Dog` |
| `$m is {name: string}` over a `mixed` or `object` subject, or an object whose `name` field is `mixed`, tainted or not declared | `E0851` | text out of `mixed` is `tainted` ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)), and a written shape says so itself: `$m is tainted {name: string}` |

Nothing else is refused. In particular a test whose answer the declaration already settles is **not**:
`int $n; $n is int` compiles and is `true`, `int $n; $n is string` compiles and is `false`, and
`int $n; $n is Request` compiles and is `false` like the rest. `is` is applicable to every subject,
because every value has a representation, and a knowable answer is not a meaningless question.

A target nothing is ever an instance of settles the same way. A `Core` **namespace** class is a name
for static members alone, so `$x is Core\Str` is `false` for every subject and every spelling that
reaches one: a member of an intersection settles the whole test, while a union answers on its live
members — `$x is int|Core\Str` is the `int` row. Deeper, the answer belongs to the position rather
than to the test, so `[] is array<Core\Str>` is `true`, an empty array having no element to fail.

Narrowing is the second reason. Once `is` narrows, a guard written inside an already-narrowed branch
is statically true by construction, and refusing that would let a flow analysis turn working code into
a compile error.

## What it narrows

`is` narrows its subject on the **true edge**, and is one of the four spellings in
[`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing) — which owns every other property of narrowing, including that it changes what
is known about a binding and never its declared type.

## Where the tags are finer than they look

`int` and `uint` are separate tags ([`types/uint`](types.md#types-uint)), so a value from a `BIGINT UNSIGNED` column
answers `is uint` and **not** `is int`; `is int|uint` tests for any integer. `string` and `bytes` are
separate the same way ([`types/string-is-utf8`](types.md#types-string-is-utf8), [`types/bytes`](types.md#types-bytes)), so binary data answers
`is bytes` and not `is string`. Both are consequences of a finer type system rather than of this
operator.

A guarded branch is cheaper with `is` than without it: the `as` a program wrote after a
`Core\Reflect::typeOf` comparison, and its throw path, are gone, because the test narrows.

**Memory:** none. `is` adds no representation, and every row reads a tag a value already carries.

**Declined:**
- **No operator, with the question asked through `Core\Reflect::typeOf`.** An equality against an
  enum case does not narrow ([`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing)), so every use pays a redundant `as` with a live
  throw path.
- **A diagnostic for a test whose answer is statically known.** It would fire on code narrowing itself
  produces. Dead branches, if they are worth reporting, are a lint over every condition, not a
  property of this operator.
- **`array<T>` accepted only in its bare form, to keep every test O(1).** `as array<T>` already
  performs the same walk and is accepted, so refusing the spelling that does not throw optimises
  nothing and misstates the cost.
- **`is callable` refused, by analogy with `Core\Reflect::TypeKind` having no `Callable` case.**
  `TypeKind`'s cases partition the tag space, and a closure is already an `Object`. `is` has no
  partition to keep, and overlapping questions are what an operator over the type grammar is for.
- **An `integer`-style spelling matching both integer tags.** It adds surface to hide the `int` and
  `uint` split rather than stating it, and `int|uint` already says it in the grammar a reader knows.

<sub>See also [`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing), [`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion), [`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed), [`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types), [`types/class-reference-sites`](types.md#types-class-reference-sites), [`types/one-type-test`](types.md#types-one-type-test).</sub>

<a id="types-narrowing"></a>

## Narrowing is flow-sensitive and branch-local, and there are exactly four spellings of it

`rule:types/narrowing`

Narrowing is flow-sensitive and **branch-local**, and there are four spellings of it: `is`, a
`== null` test, a comparison against a value of a single-value type, and `match (true)`. A `switch (true)`
narrows per arm the same way. A write inside a narrowed block widens the binding again, because the
narrowing described the value that was there, not the slot. A narrowing made before a loop holds
inside it unless the loop writes the binding somewhere — its body, its condition or a `for` step —
and then it holds nowhere in that loop, a read written before the write included, because the next
pass reaches that read after the write.

A ternary's two arms and the right operand of `&&` and `||` are branches too. The condition narrows
`$c ? $a : $b` exactly as it narrows `if ($c)` and its `else`, `&&` narrows its right operand as the
`if` block of its left, and `||` as the `else` block. Nothing it proves holds after the expression.
The edge where `A && B` holds proves both operands, so the block of `if ($a != null && $b != null)`
sees both narrowed, and the edge where `A || B` fails proves both negations, which is what narrows the
code after a guard clause `if ($a == null || $b == null) { return; }`. The other edge of each proves
only that one operand decided, and narrows nothing.

`is` is the general one — it tests a value against any type a value can inhabit, and it is the only
type test there is ([`types/type-test`](types.md#types-type-test)). Its value arm narrows too: `$x is $cls`, where `$cls` is
a `class<T>`, narrows the subject to **`T`** on the true edge, which is sound because a `class<T>`
holds `T` or an implementor of it ([`types/class-reference-sites`](types.md#types-class-reference-sites)). Every spelling narrows on
**one edge alone**, the one where the fact it tests holds: `$x != null`, `$x is T` and `$x == 1` on
their true edge, `$x == null` and `$x != 1` on their false edge, and a `!` in front swaps the two.
Subtracting a union member on the other edge is deliberately not done by any of the four: it is a
separable improvement, and one that has to be taken for all of them at once or not at all.

Nothing else narrows. In particular an equality against an enum case does not — `$m == Mode::Read`
leaves `$m` at its declared type in the branch it guards, and `$m as Mode::Read|Mode::Write` is how a
case-subset type is reached ([`types/enum-case-type`](types.md#types-enum-case-type)). Adding equality-driven narrowing would
have to be stated again for `!=`, `&&`, `||` and negation, where `as` says the same thing in one
place.

The subject of every spelling is a **binding**, named, or a **path of `readonly` properties** from
one — `$this->node`, `$app->config->parent` — where every property on the path is `readonly`. A
`readonly` property is written once, during construction ([`classes/readonly-is-written-once`](classes.md#classes-readonly-is-written-once)), so a test of it still holds at the next
read. A write to the path's root binding widens the path again, exactly as it widens the binding,
and so does passing the path itself as an `inout` argument, which the callee may write.
The narrowed read of a property keeps a run-time null check, which a narrowed binding does not: a
write the checker could not see throws a `LogicError` naming the property, and never reads `null` as
an object. A mutable property, an element or any other place is never the thing narrowed:
`$e->previous != null` proves nothing about the next read of a mutable `$e->previous`, because a
call in between may have written it, so a nullable one is reached through `?->` or bound to a
local and tested there, and `E0459`'s help on one shows both. Narrowing a `readonly` path spares a
program the copy into a local it would otherwise write before every test, at one compare and branch
per narrowed property read.

Narrowing never changes a binding's declared type ([`types/declaration`](types.md#types-declaration)); it changes what the
checker knows about it on one path. A value that has to *stay* narrowed is a second binding at the
type you want, or a checked `as` ([`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion)).

<sub>See also [`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed), [`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion), [`types/enum-case-type`](types.md#types-enum-case-type), [`types/type-test`](types.md#types-type-test), [`types/class-reference-sites`](types.md#types-class-reference-sites).</sub>

<a id="types-conversion"></a>

## `expr as T` is the only conversion, and it produces a `T` or throws

`rule:types/conversion`

There are exactly two ways to obtain a value of a different type: `expr as T`, and a second binding
declared at the type you want. `as` is **total in intent and checked in fact** — it produces a value
of the target type or it throws. It never rounds, truncates, or substitutes a default. `expr as ?T` is
the same operator over a nullable target and yields `null` exactly where `expr as T` would throw.

This is the whole conversion surface:

| conversion | behaviour |
|---|---|
| `int` ↔ `uint` | exact, or throws — a negative into `uint`, or above `i64::MAX` into `int` |
| `int` / `uint` → `float` | exact, or throws above 2^53, where `f64` stops representing every integer |
| `float` → `int` / `uint` | integral and in range, or throws. Rounding is `Core\Math::floor`/`ceil`/`round`, said out loud |
| `string` → `int` / `uint` / `float` | the whole string must be a number, or throws: no space, no text before or after it, no `_` and no hex. An integer target takes an optional `+` or `-` and decimal digits, so `"+5"` and `"007"` convert and `"-1" as uint` throws. A `float` target also takes a fraction and an exponent (`".5"`, `"5."`, `"1e3"`), and throws on `inf`, `nan` and a value too large to be finite. No leading-garbage rule, no `0` |
| anything → `string` | total for scalars; an object needs `Stringable`, or it throws. Out of `mixed` the result is `tainted string` ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)) |
| `array<T>` → `array<U>` | every element must satisfy `U`, or be an `int` or `uint` where `U` is `float`, at any depth; an O(n) walk, one tag test per element. Where every element already satisfies `U`, the result shares the one copy-on-write buffer. Where an `int` or `uint` element meets a `float`, the result is a new array of the operand's size with that element converted, exact or throwing above 2^53. An element type naming a class, an enum, a single-value type or a union is refused where it is written, `array<mixed>` being the way round it. No other operand produces an array: a union operand converts only when one of its members is an array or `mixed`, so `?string as array<string>` and `string\|int as ?array<string>` are refused where they are written |
| `int` / `uint` → `decimal` | always exact — both fit in 96 bits |
| `decimal` → `int` / `uint` | integral and in range, or throws. Rounding is `Core\Decimal::floor`/`ceil`/`round` |
| `float` → `decimal` | the shortest decimal that round-trips to that `float` — `0.1 as decimal` is `0.1` |
| `decimal` → `float` | nearest `f64`, lossy, and written like every other `as` |
| `string` → `decimal` | the whole string must be an exact decimal literal, or throws |
| `decimal` → `string` | total, and preserves scale: `19.90` renders `"19.90"` |
| `string as bytes` | total and free — valid UTF-8 is already a valid byte sequence, so the same buffer is reinterpreted |
| `bytes as string` | checked: the buffer must be well-formed UTF-8, or it throws. Never replaces, drops or substitutes an invalid byte |
| `EnumName` → its backing `int`/`uint` | total and free — the same representation, reinterpreted |
| backing type / `mixed` → `EnumName` | checked. Throws unless the value equals some case's value |
| `EnumName` → a different `EnumName` | **rejected**, even through `as`, whatever backs them; converting is a `match` naming every case |
| base type / `mixed` → a single-value type or a set of allowed values | checked against the named set ([`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types)) |
| an enum / `mixed` → a case-subset type | checked against the named cases ([`types/enum-case-type`](types.md#types-enum-case-type)) |
| `string` / `class<U>` → `class<T>` | the name must be `T` or a class that is one, or it throws. `Foo::class` is decided at compile time, and `class<T>` → `string` is total — the descriptor's own name, not the annotation's |
| `string` / `property<U>` → `property<T>` | the name must be one of `T`'s public declared properties, or it throws. A written-out name is decided at compile time, and `property<T>` → `string` is total |
| `mixed` / `object` / a union / a class → a shape | checked: the value must have every field the shape names at the named type, tested the way `$x is Shape` tests it ([`types/type-test`](types.md#types-type-test)), or it throws the `RuntimeError` a failed `as ClassName` throws. An operand that already satisfies the shape converts for free; one that holds no object, or a shape with a `secret` field, is refused where it is written. From `mixed` or `object`, or from an object whose field of that name is `mixed`, `object`, tainted or not declared, a text field must be written `tainted` — `as tainted {…}` — or the conversion is refused |
| any row above, under a qualifier | a successful checked conversion to a non-text type strips `tainted` and `secret`; a text result keeps both, and `as` is never a launderer for a value that keeps its type |
| any row above, out of `mixed` | the one place a qualifier is added: a text result is `tainted` wherever its type can carry it, and a non-text result is clean ([`security/taint-propagation`](security.md#security-taint-propagation)) |

A shape target has no second test: `as` runs the walk `is` runs, the object tag first and then one
presence probe and one tagged read per named field. So `as` succeeds exactly where `is` gives
`true`, and an `int` field fails a `float` one, because the walk compares the tag the slot holds
([`types/shape-type`](types.md#types-shape-type)). A field typed `mixed` passes whenever its key is present. An operand that
`is` would fold to `true` converts for free, and one it would fold to `false` is `E0708`, as a class
target is. The failure message names the shape by its fields, because an alias is a name for the
type and not a part of it.

A conversion the operand disproves by itself is a **compile** error rather than a run-time throw:
the target has to be a closed set and the operand has to name one value. Everything else is answered
where it runs.

`as` binds tighter than any binary operator, so `$a as int + 1` is `($a as int) + 1`. Inside a
`foreach` header the `as` belongs to `foreach`, so converting the subject takes parentheses:
`foreach (($m as array<int>) as int $v)`. Two conversions are *not* spelled with it: an `int` or
`uint` widening into a `float` position, which is implicit ([`types/implicit-widening`](types.md#types-implicit-widening)), and a
condition, which tests any type for truthiness without asking for one. The `(int)` cast syntax
is not a second spelling — it does not parse at all ([`types/no-legacy-cast`](types.md#types-no-legacy-cast)).

A conversion that throws is what keeps untrusted input from becoming a wrong but valid value. A
silent `0` for `"abc"` is often a real row id, which is the shape of an insecure direct object
reference. A throw arrives at the conversion that caused it, with a span, rather than at whatever
reads the wrong value later.

**Memory:** a shape target allocates nothing; it costs one field walk, O(fields), at each
conversion whose operand needs one.

**Declined:**
- **PHP's lossy casts kept beside `as`.** The lossy one would win by being shorter to type
  ([`types/no-legacy-cast`](types.md#types-no-legacy-cast)).

<sub>See also [`types/no-legacy-cast`](types.md#types-no-legacy-cast), [`types/implicit-widening`](types.md#types-implicit-widening), [`types/arithmetic`](types.md#types-arithmetic), [`types/unions-and-mixed`](types.md#types-unions-and-mixed).</sub>

<a id="types-no-legacy-cast"></a>

## PHP's `(T)expr` cast does not parse, and the diagnostic names the `as` that replaces it

`rule:types/no-legacy-cast`

`(int)expr`, `(uint)expr`, `(float)expr`, `(string)expr`, `(bool)expr`, `(array)expr` and
`(object)expr` are all rejected at parse time. The parser still recognises the shape — `(` a
scalar/`array`/`object` type keyword `)` — so that it can emit `E0225` naming the exact `as` spelling
to use, but it produces an error node; there is no cast node in the AST.

```nvs
(int)$x        // rejected — "use `$x as int` — it throws instead of silently truncating"
(string)$x     // rejected — "use `$x as string` — it throws instead of silently truncating"
```

The diagnostic fires only for that `(` *keyword* `)` shape in an operand position; the type keywords
keep their ordinary meaning everywhere else, and the rejected form still consumes its operand, so
`(int) !$x` leaves nothing dangling. `$x as int` is the only conversion spelling
([`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion)).

The cast would have been a second spelling of one operation, which
[`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name) refuses everywhere: it adds a second thing to teach and a
second question for every review, and buys nothing once both spellings check and throw alike. `as`
is the one kept because every other conversion is written that way, `int → uint` included, which
has no cast. The cost is that a PHP file with a cast anywhere does not parse until each one is
rewritten to `as`, a mechanical change since the operand and the target are both known from the
syntax.

**Declined:**
- **`(int)$x` as a permanent alias for `$x as int`.** It is the second spelling above.
- **A warning first and the error later.** Every refused PHP construct is a hard error from the start,
  since a warning is only for code that runs as written ([`core-api/casing-has-no-suppression`](core-api.md#core-api-casing-has-no-suppression)), and
  a staged removal would be the one exception.
- **The cast kept for `array` and `object` only.** Every target has the same `as` spelling, and
  keeping two of seven has no principled line.

<sub>See also [`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion).</sub>

<a id="types-type-alias"></a>

## A `type` alias is a transparent, compile-time-only synonym for a type expression

`rule:types/type-alias`

`type Name = TypeExpr;` declares a compile-time-only synonym for a type expression, written either at
file and namespace scope alongside `use` and `namespace` or as a member of a class, interface or enum
body ([`types/class-scoped-alias`](types.md#types-class-scoped-alias)) — never inside a method body, a block or an anonymous function's body, where
it is `E0233` by name like any other declaration written where control flow can reach it.

```nvs
type UserId = uint;
type Result = User|NotFoundError;
type Matrix = array<array<float>>;
type Point  = {x: int, y: int};
```

`TypeExpr` is any production of the type grammar ([`types/grammar`](types.md#types-grammar)) but one
([`types/alias-is-never-a-bare-class`](types.md#types-alias-is-never-a-bare-class)). The name is `PascalCase` like a class's, at both
sites and by the same check ([`core-api/identifier-casing`](core-api.md#core-api-identifier-casing)), because an alias stands where a class
name stands and reads as the type it names. The alias name is then lexically valid anywhere a class
name is, resolved by the same contextual lookup that already tells `self`/`static`/`parent` and an
enum's name apart from a class's, and reached through ordinary `use`/FQN resolution — nothing is
auto-imported.

An alias is **fully transparent, never nominal**: `UserId` and `uint` are the same type everywhere, in
both directions, needing no `as`, because after the checker resolves the alias there is only one type
there. It is not a newtype, and it has **zero runtime footprint** — nothing downstream of the checker
ever sees the alias name, not codegen, not the value layout, not `Core\Reflect::typeOf`, not an
isolate boundary crossing. That is what keeps it clear of [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name):
it creates no name a runtime observer can see.

Aliases are resolved eagerly and a cycle is a diagnostic — `type A = B; type B = A;` is rejected at
check time rather than left to loop or bottom out at `mixed`. They are non-parametric:
`type Rows<T> = …` is out of scope while user-defined generics are.

An alias exists because a mandatory annotation can be long: `array<array<int|string>>` written at
every parameter and property is noise that a short name removes. A file-scope alias does not reopen
[`classes/no-free-functions-or-constants`](classes.md#classes-no-free-functions-or-constants), which closes names that exist at run time with no class
to own them; an alias, like a `use` import, is resolved and discarded before code is generated.

**Declined:**
- **A nominal alias, a newtype that needs an explicit conversion.** A distinct type over an existing
  representation is a different feature with its own costs, and an alias is a transparent synonym
  only.

<sub>See also [`types/class-scoped-alias`](types.md#types-class-scoped-alias), [`types/alias-is-never-a-bare-class`](types.md#types-alias-is-never-a-bare-class), [`types/grammar`](types.md#types-grammar), [`types/shape-type`](types.md#types-shape-type).</sub>

<a id="types-alias-is-never-a-bare-class"></a>

## A `type` alias may not name a single bare class

`rule:types/alias-is-never-a-bare-class`

A `TypeExpr` that is nothing but one bare `ClassName`, `EnumName`, `self`, `static` or `parent` atom —
with no union, intersection, array wrapper or `?` sugar around it — is refused (`E0307`).

```nvs
type Id = SomeClass;              // rejected
type Ids = array<SomeClass>;      // fine
type Result = SomeClass|NotFound; // fine
```

The check runs at resolution, not while parsing: `type Id = SomeClass;` parses like any other alias,
and the resolver is where it becomes a diagnostic.

Allowing the bare form would be `use SomeClass as Id;` wearing the type grammar as a disguise: a
second name a *runtime* observer would plausibly expect to mean what `SomeClass` means everywhere,
which is exactly what [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name) closes. A `type` alias exists to
give a short name to a **shape** — a union, an intersection, a parameterised array, an object shape —
never to a single already-named class.

**Declined:**
- **A bare-class alias as a shorthand for a long fully-qualified name.** A `use` of the class under its
  own short name already shortens it, and the alias would be the same renaming in other syntax.

<sub>See also [`types/type-alias`](types.md#types-type-alias).</sub>

<a id="types-class-scoped-alias"></a>

## A `type` alias is also a member of a class, interface or enum, reached as `Owner::Name` and as a bare `Name` inside its owner

`rule:types/class-scoped-alias`

A `type` alias is also a member of a class, interface or enum body, taking no visibility modifier,
reached as `Owner::Name` from anywhere and as a bare `Name` inside its owner's own body, and never
inherited.

```nvs
final class Order {
    type Meta = {total: decimal, note?: string};

    public function meta(): Meta { … }          // the short form, inside the owner
}

function show(Order::Meta $m): void { … }       // the qualified form, anywhere
```

Everything [`types/type-alias`](types.md#types-type-alias) says about an alias holds here unchanged: it is transparent in
both directions, it is erased before codegen, a cycle is a diagnostic, and it may not name one bare
class-shaped atom ([`types/alias-is-never-a-bare-class`](types.md#types-alias-is-never-a-bare-class)). The member is accepted in a class, an
interface and an enum body alike — an interface's alias is not a contract an implementor satisfies,
and an enum's alias has nothing to do with its cases.

- **No visibility, ever.** A modifier run or an attribute group written in front of a body's `type`
  is `E0133`. Visibility restricts reaching a name a running program has, and an alias has none; a
  `private` alias would hide the name while leaving the type it expands to writable by anyone.
- **No inheritance.** `Sub::Name`, where only an ancestor of `Sub` declares `Name`, is `E0405`
  naming the owner that does. A class constant is inherited because a subclass genuinely has one; an
  alias is an entry on nothing, and inheriting it would give one type as many names as its owner has
  descendants — what [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name) closes.
- **Two spellings and no third.** `self::Name` and `static::Name` in type position are not spellings
  of this member and are `E0135` where they are written, as `parent::Name` is
  ([`types/grammar`](types.md#types-grammar)). An alias is resolved before there is a receiver, so `static::` could only
  ever mean the lexical class, which the bare `Name` already says.
- **A name is one thing.** A body's alias sharing a name with a class constant, an enum case or an
  enum the same body declares ([`enums/class-scoped-enum`](enums.md#enums-class-scoped-enum)) is `E0304` at the later of the two
  declarations. `Owner::Name` in type position is therefore read as an alias, then an owned enum, then
  an enum case, then a class constant, and no program that compiles depends on that order — it exists
  so the diagnostic for a name that resolves to nothing can say what was looked for.

The member exists so a type that describes one class's data is named by its owner, as that class's
constants and methods are, and not by an owner prefix written by hand into a file-scope name
(`OrderMeta`, `InvoiceMeta`). `nvs meta --json` lists it inside its owner's entry, and the file-scope
roster holds only file-scope aliases. Its declaration is keyed by the owner's `QName` and the member
name, never by a namespace path: `Ns\Order\Meta` is also the spelling of a class `Meta` in namespace
`Ns\Order`, and the two must not share a key.

- **Memory:** nothing per request, because nothing about the member survives the checker and the
  compiled program is the one the file-scope form produces. At compile time it costs one alias-table
  entry per declaration, the same entry the file-scope form pays for.

**Declined:**
- **Aliases at file scope only.** Every program would pay for it with owner prefixes spelled by hand,
  to save one member kind in the parser.
- **An owner-scoped alias that is a distinct type from its expansion.** That is a newtype, and an alias
  is transparent ([`types/type-alias`](types.md#types-type-alias)).
- **A parametric `type Rows<T> = …` in a body.** It is out of scope at both sites while user-defined
  generics are ([`types/type-alias`](types.md#types-type-alias)).

<sub>See also [`types/type-alias`](types.md#types-type-alias), [`types/alias-is-never-a-bare-class`](types.md#types-alias-is-never-a-bare-class), [`types/shape-type`](types.md#types-shape-type).</sub>

<a id="types-callable-values"></a>

## `callable` is satisfied by an anonymous function or a method reference and by nothing else, and no object is callable  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:types/callable-values`

`callable` is satisfied by exactly two kinds of value: an anonymous function (`fn (...) => ...`) and a
method reference — `Core\Str::length`, `$user->getName(...)`, `self::helper` (early-bound),
`static::helper` (late-bound), one form per receiver ([`expressions/method-reference`](expressions.md#expressions-method-reference)). A method
reference names a member, and the checker records the resolved target. Both make the same kind of
value, a callable.

Three other ways to name a function are refused where they are written, each with a diagnostic naming the
replacement: a bare name string (`'strlen'`), a `"Class::method"` string, and a `[$obj, 'method']`
array. Two further refusals fall out of the same rule: `new C(...)` is `E0740`, because `new` names a
class rather than a callee, and `$m->method(...)` on a `mixed` receiver is `E0732`, because a callable
outlives the site and there is no class present to read a callee off
([`types/erased-member-access`](types.md#types-erased-member-access)).

**There is no `__invoke`.** `$obj(...)` is a diagnostic whenever `$obj` is not itself a callable,
whatever methods the object's class declares, and a method named `__invoke` does not compile, like
every leading-underscore name ([`classes/no-leading-underscore-identifiers`](classes.md#classes-no-leading-underscore-identifiers)). `()` therefore
stays one thing rather than a second operator any class can opt into. `$obj(...)` names no method at
the call site, which is the hidden dispatch [`classes/no-call-magic`](classes.md#classes-no-call-magic) closes, and a class that
could opt into `()` would be a second operator-overloading mechanism beside the one narrow,
interface-gated one ([`classes/comparable`](classes.md#classes-comparable)).

A callee the checker cannot prove is a callable — one typed `mixed`, or a `?callable` that holds
`null` — is checked when the call runs. A value that is not a callable throws a catchable `LogicError`
naming what it is, the class the same call throws for an argument of the wrong type.

The rule is the same at every position typed `callable` — a parameter, a property, a return type, a
stdlib signature: the argument must already be a callable by the time it arrives, never a string, an
array, or an object the checker would have to interpret.

A string or array callable resolves by name at the call site, against whatever happens to be declared
there, so neither a reader, the checker nor an editor can follow it without reimplementing PHP's
lookup. A callable made by an anonymous function or a method reference always leads back to the place
that made it, so "go to definition" on any callable value lands on real code.

**Declined:**
- **Keeping all five of PHP's callable shapes**, an object with `__invoke` and the three by-name
  spellings beside the anonymous function. That keeps the by-name path next to the syntax that
  already replaces it.
- **Keeping `__invoke` as the one exception.** It is the hidden dispatch and the second
  operator-overloading mechanism above.
- **A dedicated `MethodRef` or `FunctionRef` type.** A second type with no behaviour of its own adds
  surface and nothing else ([`types/callable-is-the-only-function-type`](types.md#types-callable-is-the-only-function-type)).

<sub>See also [`types/anonymous-function`](types.md#types-anonymous-function), [`types/callable-is-the-only-function-type`](types.md#types-callable-is-the-only-function-type), [`types/callable-signature`](types.md#types-callable-signature).</sub>

<a id="types-anonymous-function"></a>

## `fn` is the only way to write an anonymous function, with an expression body or a block body

`rule:types/anonymous-function`

`fn` is the only way to write an anonymous function, in two body shapes:

```nvs
fn($x) => $x + 1                            // expression body, implicit return
fn($x) => { $y = $x + 1; return $y * 2; }   // block body, explicit `return` required
fn(int $x): int => $x + 1                   // typed either way
```

`function (...) {...}` and `function (...) use (...) {...}` do not parse; the diagnostic names `fn`.
A block-bodied `fn` still declares its return type (`E0450`) — inferring one would be whole-body
return-type inference, which this language does not do. `static fn` is diagnosed as a `function`
anonymous function.

Each parameter of a `fn` takes exactly one argument. A `...` or a default on one is `E0877` at the
parameter: a call through `callable` passes one argument for each declared parameter and checks only
that there are enough, so a variadic parameter would collect no list and a default would never be read.
A function that takes many values declares an `array<T>` parameter.

This removes a second spelling rather than adding a capability: a method reference and the
expression-bodied anonymous function already produce exactly the value a block-bodied anonymous function does
([`types/callable-values`](types.md#types-callable-values)). Capture is never written ([`types/implicit-capture`](types.md#types-implicit-capture)), and an
anonymous function that needs to call itself carries a self-name instead
([`types/anonymous-function-self-name`](types.md#types-anonymous-function-self-name)). The block body is not a new form: PHP's arrow function
never grew one only because it was added after the `function` literal, and nothing requires `fn` to
keep that restriction.

**Declined:**
- **Keeping both `function (...) {...}` and `fn`.** Two spellings of one value
  ([`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name)).
- **A bare `($x) => ...` without `fn`.** A parenthesised list before `=>` cannot be told apart from a
  parenthesised expression without a cover grammar; `fn` decides it from one token.
- **Filling a missing argument from a parameter's default, or collecting a `...` into a list.** A
  `callable` carries its arity and its parameter tags, never its defaults, so each call through it
  would have to read the declaration at run time. One argument for each parameter keeps the call as it
  is.
- **Blocks that are expressions, returning their last value.** That decides statements against
  expressions for the whole language to save one `return`.

<sub>See also [`types/implicit-capture`](types.md#types-implicit-capture), [`types/anonymous-function-self-name`](types.md#types-anonymous-function-self-name), [`types/callable-values`](types.md#types-callable-values).</sub>

<a id="types-callable-signature"></a>

## A `callable` type may name its parameters, and must then name its return type

`rule:types/callable-signature`

A `callable` type may name its parameters and its return type:

```nvs
callable(User, string): string   $format;
callable(): void                 $onExit;
callable                         $anything;
```

The **return type is mandatory** — `callable(int)` with no return says strictly less than bare
`callable` while costing a second spelling of "unknown". `void` and `never` are writable there as in
any other return position. **No parameter names**: `callable(int $x): string` does not parse, because
a name in the type would imply calling through the value by name, which nothing supports.

Bare `callable` remains the **top of the callable lattice** — a callable whose signature is unknown.
Every callable type is assignable to it, calling through one keeps the dynamic path and its
per-argument tag check, and nothing existing changes meaning. Narrowing is opt-in. Where a call
reaches a callable whose type names its parameters, the arguments are proven at compile time and the
per-argument tag check is **not emitted**; the metadata stays on every callable, because bare `callable`
still needs it and an anonymous function does not know where it is written which kind of site will call it.

**The reason is safety, not convenience.** A compiled callable reads each argument at its own declared
representation, so a mismatched argument is reinterpreted: an `int` read as a string pointer is an
arbitrary dereference, not a fault. A bare `callable` guards that with a runtime tag check per
argument, per call. A written signature discharges the same guard at compile time, as an error where
the mismatch is written. `Core\Arr::map($ints, fn (string $s): string => $s)` over an `array<int>`
does not compile.

**A parameter that names a class is checked against the argument's ancestry at the callable's
entry.** The tag check compares representations, and every class name, `object` and a shape share one
tag, so it accepts an instance of an unrelated class. A named-class binding is read and written at a
fixed offset against its label, so that acceptance is a type confusion and not a wrong answer: one
wrong callback can write an `int` over a `string` field, and the next read dereferences it. That is
security and request isolation. Every other position is checked where it is written, and an erased
receiver carries no label at all ([`types/erased-member-access`](types.md#types-erased-member-access)), so the callable's entry is the
one place nothing else looked. The body's first block runs the same class test `$x is C` runs on each
class-declared parameter, and a miss throws a `LogicError`. A parent class and an implemented
interface accept the instance an exact class does.

Two things the entry check does not do. A `?C` parameter is unchecked on both lines: it erases to a
tagged value before any class survives, the same nothing `mixed` gets. And the error does not name the
class that arrived, because no compiled instruction reads an object's class name, and adding one is a
new value shape for the sake of a message.

The parameter list needs no trial parse: a `(` after `callable` in a type position can only open a
parameter list, because a type position has no call syntax to confuse it with.

The binding-site variant that stood in for a callback's return type is retired: every `Core`
signature that used it writes an ordinary `callable(T, string): U` instead, and a type variable binds
by walking into it the way it walks into `array<T>`. The restriction that a shape's every field be a
*written* anonymous function goes too, because a `callable(): T`-typed variable now carries what the
field needs. The shape-of-callables type that `Core\Task::all` takes stays, as a bound and nothing
more: no type variable can be bounded, and without it `Task::all(5)` would compile and answer `mixed`.
What it accepts is ordinary assignability, and what it binds is the same structural walk.

- **Memory:** none. A written signature adds no runtime representation, no heap shape and no
  per-callable growth. The parameter tags and the arity stay on every callable value. The entry
  check spends one scan of the argument's ancestry per class-declared parameter per call, and
  allocates nothing.

**Declined:**
- **Angle brackets, `callable<User, string, string>`.** The return type would be positional and
  unmarked, and `callable<void>` reads as taking a `void`. Seeing the return type is worth more than
  matching the bracket shape of `array<T>`.
- **An optional return type.** `callable(int)` would be a third level of partial knowledge that still
  cannot bind a result type variable, so it buys argument checking at the price of a second syntax.
- **Optional and variadic parameters in a callable type.** `callable(int, ?string = null): void` and
  `callable(int, ...string): void` do not parse. The prefix rule ([`types/callable-arity`](types.md#types-callable-arity))
  already covers a callback that ignores trailing arguments, and no `Core` callback's own arity
  varies.
- **`Closure` as a second name for a typed signature.** One function type is enough
  ([`types/callable-is-the-only-function-type`](types.md#types-callable-is-the-only-function-type)).
- **Name-keyed access for every named-class property.** It closes the same hole everywhere, but it
  spends latency in every program, most of which never write an anonymous function.
- **A class channel in the parameter tags.** A per-callable list of descriptors would spend an
  allocation at every anonymous function literal to answer a question the body's first block asks
  for free.

<sub>See also [`types/callable-arity`](types.md#types-callable-arity), [`types/callable-variance`](types.md#types-callable-variance), [`types/anonymous-function-parameter-inference`](types.md#types-anonymous-function-parameter-inference), [`types/callable-values`](types.md#types-callable-values).</sub>

<a id="types-callable-arity"></a>

## A callable satisfies a callable type when its arity is at most the type's, matched from the left

`rule:types/callable-arity`

A callable of arity *n* satisfies `callable(T₁..Tₘ): R` when **`n ≤ m`**, and only the first *n*
parameter types are compared. An arity greater than *m* is refused where it is written.

```nvs
map(array<T> $a, callable(T, string): U $fn): array<U>

Core\Arr::map($users, fn($u) => $u->name);               // 1 ≤ 2 — $u is User
Core\Arr::map($users, fn($u, $k) => "{$k}: {$u->name}"); // 2 ≤ 2 — $k is string
Core\Arr::map($users, fn($u, $k, $x) => …);              // refused
```

A **call** through such a type passes *m* arguments, not *n*: what the value holds is the type's
business and not the call site's, and the runtime hands that callable only the leading arguments it
declares. A site passing fewer would leave one of the callable's own parameters unfilled, which is a
fault below the language rather than a throw, so it is refused where it is written (`E0809`).

This is not tolerance invented for convenience: the runtime already hands a callee only the arguments
it declares, which is what lets a one-parameter callback satisfy the `Core` convention that every
callback is offered value *and* key. The type system describes that behaviour. An exact-arity rule
would instead grow an unused `$key` parameter across every callback ever written.

**Declined:**
- **Exact arity.** Every callback in every program and test would grow an unused parameter, and the
  runtime's trimming would become dead code.
- **Exact arity for a typed `callable`, trimming for a bare one.** Two arity rules, chosen by whether
  the callee annotated, which is invisible at the call site where the error appears. Adding a
  signature would then break every short callback.

<sub>See also [`types/callable-signature`](types.md#types-callable-signature), [`types/callable-variance`](types.md#types-callable-variance).</sub>

<a id="types-callable-variance"></a>

## A callable's parameters are contravariant and its return type covariant

`rule:types/callable-variance`

A callable type's **parameters are contravariant** and its **return type covariant**:

```nvs
callable(User, string): string   $slot;

fn (User $u, string $k): string => …    // exact           — accepted
fn (mixed $u, mixed $k): string => …    // wider params    — accepted
```
